title: God Promises David a Royal Line
overview: David offers to build a temple for God, and God answers that David's son will build it while God builds David a lasting family of kings.

parts.label: David wants to build (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: David lives in a palace of costly cedar wood, while the ark, the sacred chest that stood for God's presence with Israel, still sits in a tent. The prophet Nathan assumes this is a good plan and tells him to go ahead.

parts.label: God says not you (vv. 3-6)
parts.note: That night God tells Nathan that David will not be the builder, since from the time of leaving Egypt God has moved from place to place with his people in a tent and never asked any leader for a temple. The point seems to be that God is not tied to one place and has never demanded a grand building.

parts.label: From shepherd to king (vv. 7-10a)
parts.note: God reminds David that he took him from looking after sheep and made him king, giving him victories and fame. He also promises Israel a settled home, free from the raids and oppression they had known since the days of the judges, the local leaders before the kings.

parts.label: A house for David (vv. 10b-12)
parts.note: Here the word "house" turns around: David wanted to build God a house (a temple), but God will build David a house (a family line of kings). One of David's sons, understood to be Solomon, will build the temple, and God will make his throne last forever.

parts.label: Father and son (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: God promises to treat this king like a son and never take his love away, as he did from Saul, the king before David. David's descendants ruled for about four centuries until the Babylonian conquest, and Christians read the "forever" promise as fulfilled in Jesus, who is called the son of David.

parts.label: David's prayer of thanks (vv. 15-27)
parts.note: David sits before God, amazed that someone from his humble family has been given such a future, and he praises God as unlike any other. He then asks God to do just as he has promised, so that God's name and David's family line will both endure.

disagreement: Christians differ on how directly the "forever" promise speaks of Jesus: some read it first as a promise about Solomon and his royal line, with "forever" meaning a long but limited time, while others see it as pointing beyond Solomon to the Messiah from the start.
think: David's plan was turned down but answered with something he had not asked for; has a "no" in your own life ever led somewhere you would not have chosen for yourself?
